analysis.one_liner: Routes all asbestos lawsuits through a national medical screening corporation and mandatory mediation before anyone can reach a courtroom.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee after its May 1998 referral; the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with no markup and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal Asbestos Resolution Corporation with exclusive power over who may sue for asbestos injuries. No one could file an asbestos lawsuit without first getting a certificate of medical eligibility from the corporation and completing mediation. It would ban class actions without each defendant's consent, abolish punitive damages, and bar awards for emotional distress, medical monitoring, and increased risk of future disease. It also caps claimant attorneys' fees at 25%, while defendants pay the corporation's costs and lose statute-of-limitations defenses.
analysis.who_benefits: Asbestos manufacturers and other defendants, along with their liability insurers, gain the most: no punitive damages, no emotional-distress or medical-monitoring awards, no class actions without their consent, and a medical gatekeeper that screens out claims that do not meet fixed criteria. Seriously impaired claimants also get something: an administrative track intended to pay faster, an end to statute-of-limitations defenses, and preservation of the right to sue later if a nonmalignant condition turns into cancer.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Asbestos Resolution Corporation with exclusive authority to set medical eligibility rules and run mediation and arbitration for all asbestos personal-injury claims [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings state that less than half of asbestos litigation costs reach claimants, more than 150,000 cases are pending, and litigation has bankrupted more than 15 companies, and the bill is designed to steer money toward seriously impaired claimants instead of unimpaired filers [S3].
It abolishes statute-of-limitations and other timeliness defenses for claims that were timely when the act passed, and lets a nonmalignant settlement be followed by a later cancer claim [S3].

Defendants get procedural protections: no class or collective action without each defendant's consent, a presumption that the corporation's eligibility finding is correct, and a 10% penalty against defendants only if their mediation offer falls more than 25% short of the final award [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and families exposed to asbestos pay if the bill passes: those whose conditions do not meet the fixed medical criteria are locked out of court entirely, and even successful claimants lose punitive damages, emotional-distress awards, medical monitoring, and recovery for fear of future cancer. Claimant attorneys' fees are capped at 25% of any recovery, and defendants finance the screening system through assessments.

drawbacks.text: The certificate of medical eligibility becomes a hard prerequisite for any lawsuit, so a person exposed to asbestos who does not meet the statutory criteria — including strict latency periods of 10 to 12 years and specific exposure-year calculations that do not count exposure after 1979 in most cases — has no access to a jury at all [S3].

The bill eliminates punitive damages in every asbestos case and bars recovery for emotional distress, medical monitoring, and increased risk of disease, reducing compensation even for people who qualify under the medical criteria [S3].
Class actions and other collective proceedings are barred unless every defendant consents, removing a tool that lets large groups of similarly exposed workers share legal costs [S3].

Supporters would answer that the current system is genuinely broken by their own findings — under half of litigation dollars reach claimants, verdicts are arbitrary, and unimpaired claims divert money from the seriously ill — but the bill's remedy shifts the cost of fixing that onto the sickest claimants rather than onto defendants [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real dysfunction: asbestos dockets were clogged, slow, and expensive, with much of the money going to lawyers and unimpaired claimants. But its remedy is one-sided. The provisions that help claimants — faster payment, no timeliness defenses, preserved future cancer claims — sit alongside provisions that cut total compensation (no punitive damages, no emotional-distress or medical-monitoring awards) and put a corporation controlled by a presidentially appointed board between sick workers and the courts, with strict medical cutoffs that would bar some genuinely exposed people from ever suing. On balance the design favors defendants, with the savings coming out of claimants' recoveries rather than out of defendants' overall exposure in a transparent way.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never marked it up or reported it, and it died when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Hyde introduced the bill on May 20, 1998, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S5].

That was the only action ever taken: the bill received no subcommittee or committee action, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action recorded in its history before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1] [S5].
Thirteen House members — 10 Republicans and 3 Democrats — cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, workers exposed to asbestos kept the existing court system, including access to juries, class actions, punitive damages, and emotional-distress awards, without passing through a federal screening gate. Asbestos defendants kept the existing system too, with its high litigation costs but also its full exposure. No party to this fight got the change it wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Asbestos claimants kept full court access

sides.party_line_note: The 13 cosponsors split 10 Republican to 3 Democratic, and the sponsor was the Republican committee chairman; because the bill never reached a floor vote, there is no roll-call record of broader partisan or bipartisan support.

industries.note: The bill would strip out punitive damages, emotional-distress and medical-monitoring awards, and collective lawsuits, while a medical gatekeeper screens claimants — all of which shrinks defendants' total liability. The savings come directly out of what exposed workers and their families could recover.
Insurers who cover asbestos defendants would face smaller and more predictable payouts once claims passed through screening, mandatory mediation, and the ban on punitive damages.

The bill caps claimant attorneys' total fees and expenses at 25% of any recovery and requires a medical certificate and mediation before suit, shrinking both the volume and the payout of asbestos work. Claimants would lose access to court at the same time, so the industry's loss partly overlaps with the public's.
The bill expressly makes itself inapplicable to existing court-supervised asbestos trusts, except by election, leaving those trusts outside the new screening system.
